---
title: "Radix Sort"
description: "CLRS-inspired worked lesson on Radix Sort: numerical substitution, invariants, original code and complexity."
---

## Understand the actual problem

**LeetCode 164 — Maximum Gap (integer sorting strategies).**

Sort keys one digit at a time using a STABLE digit sort. Least-significant-digit order works because later higher-digit passes preserve previous lower-digit ordering for ties.

## First try the obvious approach

If keys have fixed-width digits, a comparison tree does more general work than required.

The goal is not to memorise a data structure. It is to identify which partial result the next operation can reuse.

## Mathematical relationship, explained immediately

$$
x=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1} x_j B^j
$$

**Symbol by symbol:** x is a nonnegative integer, B is numeric base (10 for decimal), d number of digits, x_j digit at position j counted from the right.

**Calculate with real numbers:** For 237 in base 10, digits are x₀=7, x₁=3, x₂=2. Therefore 237=7×10⁰+3×10¹+2×10²=7+30+200.

Read the equation and the calculation as one explanation. If the numbers do not make sense, do not skip ahead to code.

## How the algorithm emerges

1. Identify what answer you would compute by hand for the smallest instance.
2. Store exactly that piece of information when moving to the next step.
3. Update the stored information after one input event or query.
4. Check the invariant before returning a result; consider boundary values and ties.

**Correctness argument:** After sorting by the first j digits, the array is ordered by those positions. A stable sort of digit j preserves lower-position order among keys that share this higher digit.

## Code, but only after the reasoning

Here is a standalone, original JavaScript demonstration:

~~~js
const a=[21,13,12,22];
const byOnes=[...a].sort((x,y)=>(x%10)-(y%10));
const result=byOnes.sort((x,y)=>(Math.floor(x/10)%10)-(Math.floor(y/10)%10));
console.log(result); // [12,13,21,22] (modern JS sort is stable)
~~~

This shows a deliberately minimal case; the chapter explains the invariant needed to extend it into a full implementation.

## Count the work rigorously

**Time and memory:** O(d(n+B)) time with counting sort per digit; n numbers, d digits, B possible digit values.

**The misleading shortcut:** If the per-digit sort is unstable, lower-digit results can be destroyed; negative integers and variable-width strings need an explicit representation policy.

A common interview error is to mistake a nested loop for quadratic complexity. For a monotonic stack/queue, one item is removed at most once, so total work is linear. Conversely, a sorted data structure is not automatically fast for every possible operation.
